concrete_scene.heading: Worked threat-ledger comparison: three successes that mean different things
concrete_scene.actor_or_system: Three literature-grounded model-security attack traces and their downstream owners
concrete_scene.attempted_action: Compare training-data extraction, conditional backdoor persistence, and cross-channel defense externality without collapsing them into one robustness score.
concrete_scene.observable_outcome: The traces yield three distinct bounded outcomes: memorized-sequence disclosure, persistence of a constructed trigger-conditioned policy, and a defense-induced cross-channel weakness.
concrete_scene.failed_or_tested_boundary: The comparison tests whether a generic attack-success label can preserve checkpoint, attacker, objective, utility, recovery, and harmed-party differences; it cannot.
concrete_scene.residual_owner: Privacy and incident response, checkpoint-lineage repair, and sensor or system-security owners retain different residuals for the three traces.
concrete_scene.evidence_boundary: All outcomes are source-reported and configuration-bound; the comparison is not a local reproduction, shared benchmark, universal robustness result, or support-state promotion.

worked_trace.heading: Worked threat-ledger comparison: three successes that mean different things
worked_trace.maximum_inference: The three primary-source notes show why different attack objectives require different ledgers and owners; they establish no local defense performance, general robustness, or secure-deployment authority.

counterexample_or_simpler_baseline: The simpler baseline labels any red-team finding as model insecurity, or any failed attack as robustness. The chapter keeps the exact objective, access, budget, effect, utility cost, recovery, and residual instead.
readable_claim: Model security is not one robustness score. It is a checkpoint-specific account of who attacked which surface, with what access and budget, what changed, what the defense cost, and what remained exposed.
normative_rule: Admit a security conclusion only when the attack record binds model and serving identity, attacker capability, objective, budget, adaptation, attempt denominator, clean utility, observed harm, recovery, and residual ownership. A missing field narrows the conclusion; it cannot be filled by a benchmark average or a failed attack.

formal_binding.anchor: versioned model-threat contract and attack/defense ledger

caveat_consolidation.local_caveat: The worked comparison states once that its three outcomes come from separate source-reported settings and are not one shared benchmark.
caveat_consolidation.consolidated_disposition: Attack-specific reachability, transfer, detector, defense, recovery, and universal-robustness limits remain beside the mechanism sections that need them and in the chapter guardrail.

bookkeeping_surface_disposition: The four-column comparison stays because objective, outcome, disposition, and residual are the argument; validator inventories and formal mutation counts remain in evidence surfaces.

editorial_diagnostics.mega_sentence_disposition: The reader claim and operational rule split the formal ledger bundle into readable purpose and admission logic.
editorial_diagnostics.hedge_disposition: Repeated generic caution was not deleted; the new scene consolidates its shared source-reported boundary once and preserves attack-specific limits.
editorial_diagnostics.table_disposition: The comparison table is retained as an argument-bearing distinction among attacks, not as a status inventory.

non_claims: The comparison does not reproduce any of the three source-reported attacks.
The comparison does not establish general vulnerability, robustness, or defense efficacy.
The editorial revision does not move chapter-core support or release state.
